extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom style guide providing preferred/avoidance language, capitalization, naming and context guidance for reporting about people, religions, identities, disabilities, cultures and institutions. Entries give definitions, usage notes and examples for each term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referring to people confined in correctional facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use constructions that include “person” or “people,” a subject’s name and/or fixed biographical characteristics like age or state when referring to people confined in correctional facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred examples: incarcerated people; imprisoned people; people in prison; people in jail; people jailed in X facility; formerly incarcerated people. Use specific forms when possible: John Doe, who was incarcerated at FCI Memphis; Jane Doe, who is serving 12 years in FCI Dublin; A 34-year-old detained in Los Angeles County Jail; Imprisoned in 1989, Joe Doe has filed an appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: inner city
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'inner city' as it has been used as a euphemism for lower-income residential districts and sometimes (but not exclusively) for Black neighborhoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use neutral adjectives like city center, downtown or central urban when referring to city neighborhoods and use terms like under-resourced or low-income when referring to neighborhoods or communities with high poverty rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: insane asylum / mental health hospital / psychiatric hospital
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'insane asylum' is outdated and objectionable for hospitals that cared for people with mental illness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer mental health hospital or psychiatric hospital to describe medical facilities devoted to treating people with mental disabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: insane, incompetent
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'insane,' 'insanity' and 'mentally deranged' are informal, can be offensive, and conflate legal and medical concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use medical terms mental illness or mental disorder. Note: in U.S. criminal law, 'insanity' is a legal question, not a medical one. Use 'insane' or similar only in quotations or when directly referring to a legal defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: inscrutable
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution: 'inscrutable' is a synonym for 'mysterious' but considered a racially charged adjective, particularly when used to describe Asians or Asian Americans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid racially charged descriptors; choose neutral alternatives that do not invoke stereotype.

rubrics_metrics.name: institutional racism
rubrics_metrics.description: When policies and practices put people who are not of the dominant race at a disadvantage; refers to structures and policies rather than necessarily intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term for disadvantages in government, business, education, media and other systems. Provide examples (housing policies, hiring, school-discipline practices). Note relationship to systemic racism and White privilege; explain that calling an institution racist may refer to structural outcomes rather than individual intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: intellectual disability
rubrics_metrics.description: A disability involving significant limitations in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior that typically develops before age 18 (AAIDD definition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use people-first language: 'a person with an intellectual disability' rather than calling someone 'intellectually disabled.' Includes note about IQ thresholds and distinction from congenital disorders such as Down syndrome.

rubrics_metrics.name: intelligent design
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition: the belief that some aspects of life are so complex they must reflect the design of a conscious intelligence; often associated with creationism and rejection of evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe proponents' positions accurately; note that proponents do not identify the designer but many assume God; contextualize relation to evolution and creationism.

rubrics_metrics.name: interdenominational
rubrics_metrics.description: A congregation or organization formally under the jurisdiction of more than one denomination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use as a synonym for nondenominational.

rubrics_metrics.name: interfaith
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities or events that draw people from entirely different religious traditions (e.g., Christians, Jews, Buddhists, Muslims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not a synonym for ecumenical, which refers to multiple Christian traditions; use interfaith for multiple religions.

rubrics_metrics.name: internment, Japanese
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to the World War II incarceration of roughly 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry in U.S. 'relocation centers'; two-thirds were U.S. citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some advocates prefer the term 'incarceration' instead of 'internment' as a more accurate depiction. Provide historical context (forced sale of homes/businesses, last internees released in 1946) and link to additional resources (Japanese American National Museum).

rubrics_metrics.name: interpreters
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution when a subject speaks limited English and family members are used as interpreters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using family members as interpreters because they may edit or fail to translate fully; if deadline permits, have an independent native speaker review recordings for accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: intersectionality
rubrics_metrics.description: A lens recognizing that identities (gender, race, class, sexual orientation, etc.) interact and cannot be examined in isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the concept to explain how someone can experience both privilege and oppression simultaneously and to clarify intersecting effects in individuals' lives and social systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: intersex (adj.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Umbrella term for people born with reproductive/sexual anatomy or chromosome patterns not classifiable as typically male or female (also called Differences of Sex Development, DSD).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the outdated/derogatory term 'hermaphrodite.' Do not conflate intersex conditions with being transgender; the two are separate though they may overlap for some individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: intifada
rubrics_metrics.description: An Arabic term meaning shaking, uprising or insurrection, commonly used for Palestinian resistance against Israeli occupation of Gaza and the West Bank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize there are distinct intifadas marked by specific starting events; use term with historical specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically used to denote a person made weak or disabled by illness or injury, but now widely viewed as offensive because it implies lack of ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'invalid' to describe a person with a disability except in direct quotes; use more precise, respectful terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iranian names
rubrics_metrics.description: A Persian or Iranian name typically consists of a given name (sometimes more than one) followed by a family name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sensitive to naming conventions and cultural contexts; note historical examples and spellings when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Islam (usage & titles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Background on Islam: origin, branches (Sunni, Shiite), lack of central authority and diversity of theological/legal interpretations; guidance on capitalization and use of titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize Islamic titles when used before a name and lowercase otherwise. Use title and full name on first reference and only the person's last name thereafter. Understand differences in usage of titles (e.g., imam, sheikh, mullah, mujtahid, ayatollah, mufti, grand mufti) and regional variation. Avoid assuming Arabs = Muslims or Muslims = Arabs; clarify distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Islamic (adj.) vs Islamist
rubrics_metrics.description: Islamic is an adjective describing the religion of Islam and is not synonymous with Islamist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Islamic' to mean relating to Islam; reserve 'Islamist' for advocates/supporters of political movements that favor reordering government/society according to Islamic law (see Islamist entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Islamic fundamentalist
rubrics_metrics.description: The label 'fundamentalist' applied to religious adherents often implies political conservatism and sometimes extremism; it's an American construct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming religion is the sole basis for political actions; attribute political actions to specific groups, governments or parties when appropriate; avoid pejorative constructions such as 'Muslim bomb.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Islamist
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow AP style: an 'advocate or supporter of a political movement that favors reordering government and society in accordance with laws prescribed by Islam.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use as a synonym for Islamic fighters, militants, extremists or radicals. Where possible be specific and name affiliations (e.g., al-Qaida-linked, Hezbollah, Taliban). Recognize that those who view the Quran as a political model span a range from mainstream politicians to militants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Islamophobia
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and prejudice against Muslims based on the idea that Islam is inferior and cannot adapt to modern realities; encompasses belief in irreconcilable civilizational differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize historically (existed before Sept. 11, 2001) and use supporting reporting and studies to document trends in discrimination and attacks on Muslims; link to relevant research when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issei and generational terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Issei is the Japanese term for 'first generation' immigrants; other generational terms include nisei, sansei, yonsei, shin-issei.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note capitalization differences among institutions and contexts: some capitalize generational terms in generational contexts and lowercase when referring to an individual; be attentive to style choices and specific organization preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jehovah's Witness
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious group beliefs and distinctives: use of the name Jehovah, non-recognition as Christian by some traditions, refusals (saluting flag, bearing arms, blood transfusions), no formal clergy titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use honorifics such as 'the Rev.' for Jehovah's Witnesses. Refer to evangelizing members as publishers, regular pioneers or special pioneers; gathering places called Kingdom Halls, not churches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jew (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: A follower of the Jewish faith; term can apply to men and women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Jew' for men and women. Never use 'jew' as a verb (e.g., 'he jewed me down') — that usage is offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jews for Jesus
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization founded by Jews who converted to evangelical Christianity and identify as Messianic Jews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not group Messianic Jews or Jews for Jesus with mainstream Jews in stories or listings; clearly state they are Christian by faith though Jewish by culture/ethnicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: jihad
rubrics_metrics.description: Arabic word meaning 'struggle' or 'striving'; traditionally inward spiritual struggle but also used historically for defensive military action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid translating jihad simply as 'holy war'—explain nuances and note majority of Muslims do not use it to mean holy war; contextualize modern militant uses and condemnations by mainstream Islam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jim Crow
rubrics_metrics.description: Historic laws enforcing strict racial segregation and disenfranchisement primarily in the South for roughly 80 years; term originates from a minstrel routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide historical examples of segregation in schools, public amenities, transportation, housing, etc. Contextualize the origin of the term (Daddy Rice minstrel show) and its role as a racial epithet and system of oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judaism (overview & branches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic description of Judaism, its history, beliefs and major branches (Reform, Conservative, Orthodox, Reconstructionist, Jewish Renewal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying branches, explain distinctive practices and representative organizations (e.g., Union for Reform Judaism, Orthodox Union, Rabbinical Assembly); note diversity of belief and practice across branches and movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juneteenth
rubrics_metrics.description: Commemoration of the end of slavery originating in Galveston, Texas, on June 19, 1865; emphasizes freedom, education and achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that Juneteenth can be observed as a day, week or month with celebrations, speakers and family gatherings; provide historical origin and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kaaba
rubrics_metrics.description: The black, cube-shaped building in Mecca central to Islamic worship; pilgrims on hajj circle it during rites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred pronunciation 'KAH-bah'; provide background on history, the black stone, symbolic meaning and spelling variants (Ka'bah).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kabbalah
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrine of ancient Jewish mysticism teaching paths to understanding divine mysteries through prayer and contemplation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred spelling 'Kabbalah' and uppercase in all references.

rubrics_metrics.name: kafiyyeh
rubrics_metrics.description: A checked scarf-like head garment worn by some Arab men; traditional and cultural rather than religious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note different styles and colors may carry significance; alternate spellings include keffiyeh or kufiya.

rubrics_metrics.name: karaoke
rubrics_metrics.description: Originated in Japan in the 1970s meaning 'empty orchestra'; patrons sing along to instrumental recordings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide brief origin context and note its social popularity internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: karma
rubrics_metrics.description: In Buddhism and Hinduism, the universal law of cause and effect regarding actions across lifetimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowercase in all references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kashrut / kosher
rubrics_metrics.description: Kashrut refers to Jewish dietary laws; kosher is an adjective describing food or ritual objects that meet those standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'kashrut' for the body of laws and 'kosher' as the adjective; prefer lowercase 'kosher' in references; see both terms cross-referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: keloid
rubrics_metrics.description: A raised, dense, dome-shaped scar that can develop after skin injury; more common in people of African or Asian descent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accurate medical descriptions and be aware of demographic predispositions when relevant to reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: kesh
rubrics_metrics.description: The wearing of long, uncut hair by Sikhs as one of the Five K's (articles of faith).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe kesh as a religious symbol of respect for natural perfection; place within Sikh practice context.

rubrics_metrics.name: killing fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally refers to mass killings in Cambodia by the Khmer Rouge in the mid-1970s; can be used more broadly for any site of mass killing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide historical attribution (coined by Dith Pran) and avoid casual or metaphorical overuse that diminishes historical specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Koran / Quran spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred spelling is 'Quran' capitalized; 'Koran' should be used only if it's part of a specific title or name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt 'Quran' for general references and reserve older spellings for titles or quoted language where that form appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Korean names
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically family name first, followed by a two-part personal name; many Korean Americans adopt Western name order in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to cultural naming order and gender differences; confirm preferred ordering with sources when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ku Klux Klan (naming and references)
rubrics_metrics.description: Official name 'Knights of the Ku Klux Klan'; multiple organizations exist under that name; KKK initials acceptable on second reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize formal titles before a name (e.g., Imperial Wizard James R. Venable). Members are Klansmen or Klanswomen. Use KKK initials on second reference; identify specific Klan organizations when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: kufi
rubrics_metrics.description: A skullcap worn by some Muslims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe cultural/religious context if relevant; use accurate terminology (kufi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kwanzaa
rubrics_metrics.description: A celebration of African heritage and principles observed Dec. 26 through Jan. 1, originating in the 1960s Black Nationalist Movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain seven principles (umoja, kujichagulia, ujima, ujamaa, nia, kuumba, imani) and seven symbols; note intention to be independent of religion though some families celebrate religious holidays alongside Kwanzaa.

rubrics_metrics.name: lama (title usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Tibetan Buddhist teacher or master; capitalize when used as a title before a name or when referring to the Dalai Lama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize 'Lama' as a title before names (e.g., Lama Surya Das) and when referring specifically to the Dalai Lama.

rubrics_metrics.name: lame
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically describes difficulty walking due to leg injury, but is often used colloquially to mean weak and can be offensive regarding disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'lame' to describe a person with a disability except when quoting someone; prefer precise medical or descriptive terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laotian names
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically family name first and personal name second; often multi-syllable names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect cultural ordering and naming conventions; confirm preferences when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin@
rubrics_metrics.description: A post-internet construction intended to simplify 'Latino/Latina' or 'Latino and/or Latina' by using '@' to present both feminine and masculine endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note academic/community use (e.g., University of Wisconsin example) and link to related terms like Chican@; be aware of audience and readability concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latina / Latino (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Umbrella terms referring to U.S. residents/citizens with Latin American ancestry; 'Latina' is feminine, 'Latino' masculine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Latina(s) for women, Latino(s) for men. Note regional preferences (Latino used west of Mississippi). Federal policy treats 'Latino' as an ethnicity, not a race. Cross-reference related terms (Chicana/Chicano, Latinx, Latine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Latine
rubrics_metrics.description: A gender-neutral or non-binary alternative to Latino/Latina, replacing the vowel ending with 'e' (pronounced la-TEEN-eh).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note origins in LGBTQIA+ and feminist communities, ease of pronunciation relative to Latinx, and use in plural forms; mark as updated March 2024.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latinx
rubrics_metrics.description: A gender-neutral term using '-x' to replace gendered Spanish noun endings; pronounced 'La-teen-ex.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note limited familiarity/use among many Hispanic/Latino adults (Pew survey stats), and that it may be unfamiliar to many people; updated February 2021. Avoid using as umbrella label for an individual (do not refer to an individual as 'LGBTQ+ or Latinx' when referring to a single person).

rubrics_metrics.name: Latter-day Saints / LDS Church
rubrics_metrics.description: See Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints; 'LDS Church' acceptable on second reference; lowercase 'church' when using shortened term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use full formal name on first reference; recognize alternative usages (Mormon) and preferred organizational references.

rubrics_metrics.name: lay person
rubrics_metrics.description: A member of the laity (non-clergy); 'lay person' and 'lay people' are two words; 'layman' and 'laywoman' are one word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise terms according to gender and plurality; prefer 'lay person' when gender-neutral single usage is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lent
rubrics_metrics.description: The period of penance and fasting preceding Easter with varying observance practices across Christian denominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe timing (Ash Wednesday to Holy Thursday/Holy Saturday variations), fasting/abstinence expectations in Catholic practice, and denomination-specific differences among Protestants; provide historical context and contemporary practice differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: lesbian
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred term, noun and adjective, for women attracted to other women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some women prefer 'gay' — when possible ask the subject which term she prefers.

rubrics_metrics.name: LGBT / LGBTQ+ terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions for abbreviations: LGBT = lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender; Q can mean questioning or queer; '+' represents additional identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Diversity Style Guide recommends 'LGBTQ+' as the inclusive umbrella term. Do not refer to an individual as 'LGBT' or 'LGBTQ+'; use specific identity labels for individuals. Note updated guidance (March 2023) and reference NLGJA and GLAAD positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: lifestyle (sexual orientation)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Lifestyle' is an inaccurate term sometimes used to describe gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'lifestyle' to describe sexual orientation; explain that sexual orientation is not a 'lifestyle.' See sexual orientation, sexual preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: linguistic racism
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrimination based on accent, dialect or speech patterns, which can be overt or covert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples (mocking speech; 'You speak English well for someone who looks like you'; 'You don't sound Black'), and note that certain languages/dialects (Spanish, AAVE, etc.) may be undervalued. Added June 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: little person
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-reference to dwarf, midget, short stature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the preferred terms in entries for dwarf/short stature and avoid offensive or outdated descriptors.

rubrics_metrics.name: liturgy
rubrics_metrics.description: Has two meanings: for Western Christians a lowercase 'liturgy' is a standard set of prayers/practices; for Orthodox/Eastern Christians 'Liturgy' is capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use uppercase 'Liturgy' for Orthodox/Eastern Catholic usage and lowercase for Western Christian contexts; distinguish between liturgical and nonliturgical churches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lord (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always capitalize 'Lord' when referring to God in a monotheistic faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capitalization for reverential references (e.g., Lord Jesus, Lord Krishna).

rubrics_metrics.name: lover
rubrics_metrics.description: A term some individuals prefer for a sexual partner across orientations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives include girlfriend, boyfriend and partner; use the term the subject prefers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lubavitch / Lubavitcher
rubrics_metrics.description: A large branch of Hasidic Judaism (Chabad-Lubavitch) with historical background and leadership (the Rebbe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe beliefs/organization, alternative names (Chabad-Lubavitch), and internal practices; provide context on varying beliefs about leadership and messianic claims where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: lupus
rubrics_metrics.description: A chronic autoimmune disease that can affect skin, joints, kidneys, lungs, brain and heart; disproportionately affects Black women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accurate medical descriptions and note demographic disparities when relevant to reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lutheran
rubrics_metrics.description: Member of a Protestant denomination tracing roots to Martin Luther; major U.S. bodies include ELCA and Missouri Synod with theological differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe denominational differences and representative organizations; note variation in observance and governance.
